segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics news digest for November 7th, 2026.
We've got 19 updates, including deep dives on ROS, new battery tech, and domestic service robots.
Tune in for the latest.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: What happened to \"
Robot-as-a-Snap\"".
This segment addresses the development of an Ubuntu Robotics ecosystem using Snaps and Ubuntu Core and its implications for production robot software deployment.

Canonical has developed an Ubuntu Robotics ecosystem utilizing Snaps and Ubuntu Core, providing atomic updates and version linking for reliable robot deployment, incorporating ROS 2 extensions, observability hooks, and fleet management tools.

However, there is limited discussion within the ROS 2 community regarding the use of Snaps for shipping production robot software, as alternatives such as standard apt, Docker, or Yocto remain more frequently discussed.
The investigation examines whether strict confinement imposes limitations on necessary hardware access or if the maintenance overhead favors alternative deployment methodologies for robotics.
This development signals ongoing technical debate regarding the most efficient deployment strategies for complex robotic systems.
From Humanoids Daily, "Atlas Battery Pack to Use 70 Samsung SDI Cells, Report Says".
This report details the composition and capacity of a battery pack utilized by the Atlas humanoid robot.
The pack is formed using seventy Samsung SDI twenty-one-seven-zero cells, yielding an approximate energy capacity of one point three kilowatt-hours.
The supply chain for these components involves Samsung SDI supplying the majority of the initial cells, with LG Energy Solution also reportedly involved in the overall supply chain.
Each of these reported cells possesses a capacity of five thousand milliampere-hours.
Runtime for the robot is contingent upon factors such as task demands, payload, and computing requirements, rather than solely on the pack's total capacity.
Future developments in this area are focusing on battery swapping and the exploration of novel chemistries to extend humanoid robot operational duration.
This development signals ongoing research into power solutions for advanced artificial intelligence hardware.
From Humanoid.guide, "Tau Robotics sends humanoids into homes for paid cleaning".
This report details the deployment of humanoid robots for paid cleaning services in San Francisco and the subsequent findings from initial trials.
Tau Robotics utilizes remote human operators for much of the cleaning work while simultaneously collecting training data.
The service charges approximately sixty dollars weekly for two robots, and the trials indicated a significant dependence on reliable communication and the functionality of the operator's equipment.
The robots are four and a half feet in height and are equipped with cameras for remote operation, employing kinematic guidance for tasks such as making beds.
Initial trials revealed operational difficulties, including struggles with navigating stairs and instances where equipment shutdowns required human assistance.
The objective of these trials is to use these real-world examples to train models for more autonomous housekeeping capabilities.
This work advances the development of more capable and adaptable artificial intelligence systems for domestic tasks.
From The Robot Report, Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance.
This report details the unveiling of the Stretch Gen 2, an updated autonomous mobile trailer unloading robot designed for enhanced reliability and performance.
The new model features a modular design facilitating easy part swaps and improved durability achieved through the integration of automotive-grade connectors and continuous rotation joints.
Further upgrades include a gripper capable of multi-box picking in a single motion, which reduces service time to just hours.
The robot also incorporates onboard diagnostics and a continuously improving software platform enabling remote performance enhancements.
Customer feedback indicated that the robot provides a simple and effective user experience for heavy lifting tasks.
This development signals continued advancement in autonomous robotics and heavy industrial automation.
From TechCrunch - Robotics, Physicl raises $10 million to make the digital world real enough for robots.
This funding is allocated to utilize expertise in three-dimensional rendering to enhance robot training through realistic simulations.
The company seeks to assist model designers and robot builders in resolving training difficulties by developing more accurate digital environments.
Physicl provides tools such as Studio which enable users to generate synthetic data for training robots on intricate scenarios.
The platform focuses on automating the conversion of unstructured real-world information into high-fidelity three-dimensional representations necessary for artificial intelligence.
This methodology intends to allow robots to improve their comprehension, interaction, and manipulation of physical space.
This development signals a push toward more realistic and efficient simulation methods for advancing robotics and artificial intelligence applications.
From Humanoids Daily, "Inside Unitree's Hangzhou Factory, Robots Are Still Mostly Built by Hand".
This report details the current state of robot actuator production at Unitree's Hangzhou facility, indicating that the manufacturing process remains predominantly manual.
The company's 2025 filings show that direct labor accounted for only 8.1 percent of the cost of goods.
Production of robot actuators in the Hangzhou factory is largely accomplished through manual labor, with only a limited number of new automated lines in place.
The analysis suggests that trade barriers currently make factory automation more valuable for American manufacturers than for Unitree.
Automation is projected to increase significantly as artificial intelligence reduces the time required for programming and integration.
Investment focus is expected to shift toward developing standardized motor lines rather than concentrating solely on humanoid assembly.
This trend signals a necessary pivot in industrial investment toward foundational component standardization.
From Humanoid.guide, Embodied AI unveils the AIR humanoid robot for shared factory work, with manufacturer testing currently in progress.
This report details the introduction of the AIR robot, which is designed to handle repetitive manual tasks that change frequently in factory environments.
The robot employs a tendon-driven architecture with motors positioned in the torso and wheels to ensure stability on factory floors, prioritizing manipulation capabilities over full bipedal mobility.
The system learns tasks through observation of runs, incorporating human oversight during the initial learning phase.
Physical reliability is a primary design constraint, and the plan is to obtain CE marking by 2027.
This development signals a shift toward practical, adaptable robotics integration within industrial settings.
From CMU Robotics Institute, Team Chiron Competes in DARPA Triage Challenge Finals.
This report details the application of autonomous drones and ground robots with artificial intelligence for assessing and triaging wounded individuals during disasters.
The team's system gathers casualty data by detecting vital signs and locating injured people from a distance to assist emergency responders in prioritizing care.
The methodology involved deploying robotic systems to gather comprehensive data across disaster scenarios, aiming to create a complete picture of the scene.
This technology was developed to facilitate faster and more informed medical decisions in chaotic environments.
The overall objective is to advance autonomous systems that improve emergency response efficiency and save lives.
This advancement signals significant progress in applying robotics and artificial intelligence to critical humanitarian response operations.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, ByteDexter!".

This segment details the development of ByteDexter, a five-finger robotic research hand created by ByteDance Seed for artificial intelligence research, with a key finding in its design emphasis on dexterity and tactile sensing.
The device incorporates electric motors within the palm and utilizes rigid mechanical linkages along with passive four-bar linkages to achieve finger movement.
Tactile arrays are employed to measure normal force, and performance evaluation indicated a rating of four out of five for degrees of freedom, although strength was rated at one out of five.
This prototype is currently integrated into the GR Dexter project, which seeks to advance AI systems with humanlike robotic hands.
Further development in this area is anticipated to influence the trajectory of human-robot interaction technologies.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, REX G1!".
This report details the introduction of REX G1, RoboScience's first wheeled humanoid robot, which has demonstrated capabilities in environments such as factories and homes.
The robot measures one hundred seventy centimeters in height and weighs eighty kilograms.
It features an adjustable torso and two articulated arms capable of supporting a ten kilogram load, with a working reach spanning from zero point one to two meters.
The robot is designed to operate at a maximum speed of five kilometers per hour and maintains safety brakes on all joints.
Demonstrated functions include obstacle avoidance and the sorting of goods, indicating an early stage of development.
This advancement signals further exploration into practical, mobile robotics applications.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, GoMate Mini!".
This report details the introduction of the GoMate Mini, a humanoid robot developed by GAC Group and Huilun Technology, demonstrating advanced mobility and manipulation capabilities.

The robot stands at one hundred seventy centimeters and weighs sixty kilograms, incorporating twenty-seven degrees of freedom and the ability to switch between wheel configurations for operational flexibility and storage.
This fourth-generation humanoid platform is capable of executing tasks such as obstacle avoidance, recovering from a fall, sorting goods, and assembling products.
The prototype is currently available with a listed price of forty thousand United States dollars, with applications being explored in automotive production and public venues.
This development signals further advancements in robotic integration across various industrial and public settings.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, ARMAR 7!".

This report details the development of the ARMAR 7, a humanoid assistance robot created in 2024 by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, demonstrating capabilities in mobile manipulation within domestic assistance environments.
The robot features an omnidirectional mobile base, a bowing torso, and two torque-controlled arms equipped with integrated RGB cameras.
Measuring 175 centimeters in height and weighing 120 kilograms, the system possesses a listed strength of 12 kilograms.

Demonstrations of the robot’s functionality included obstacle avoidance, the sorting of goods, and the operation of a dishwasher, positioning it as a research platform focused on mobile manipulation tasks.
This development signals ongoing progress in applying advanced robotics to complex domestic assistance scenarios.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Honda Hand!".
This report details the assessment of the Honda Hand, a robotic research hand developed by Honda R&D in Japan, which yielded a score of four out of ten, placing it in the developing category.

The evaluation indicated that the hand scored three out of five for degrees of freedom but only one out of five for strength, emphasizing the necessity of evaluating movement and strength in robotic hand design separately.
This assessment stems from an evaluation of the prototype, which is listed at a price of twenty-four thousand US dollars.
Future developments in the AI and technology sector should focus on the distinct engineering challenges associated with dexterity and force application in robotic manipulation systems.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Tianzhen Z1!".
This report details the introduction of the Tianzhen Z1, a full-size humanoid robot developed by Tlibot in Mianyang, China, demonstrating capabilities in navigation and manipulation.

The robot measures one hundred sixty-seven centimeters in height and weighs forty-five kilograms, featuring a customizable, bionic appearance designed for public interaction and supporting up to forty active degrees of freedom excluding the hands.
The system demonstrates functionality in obstacle avoidance for navigation and the sorting of goods for manipulation tasks.
The robot is currently listed as a prototype with a skill score of two out of ten, indicating early-stage performance.
For exhibition, commercial, or research applications, the prototype is available at a price of thirty-five thousand United States dollars.
This development suggests ongoing progression in the field of humanoid robotics and practical application of advanced AI systems.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Gento Luna!".
This report details the specifications and current status of the wheeled humanoid robot Gento Luna.

The robot features a folding structure capable of reducing its height from one hundred seventy centimeters to seventy-nine centimeters, weighing ninety kilograms and possessing twenty-six degrees of freedom.
Each arm has seven degrees of freedom and a lifting capacity of six kilograms.
The device is equipped with three-dimensional LiDAR for obstacle avoidance and articulated arms designed for sorting goods and folding textiles.
Force-controlled electric joints utilize compliant impedance control for physical interaction.
Gento Luna is presently categorized as a prototype with a skill score of three out of ten, targeting applications in commercial services and education.
This development indicates ongoing progress in creating adaptable physical interaction systems within robotics.
From RoboPapers, "Ep#115: Delta-0 (Δ₀): A New Chapter in Humanoid Intelligence"
reports on a new humanoid foundation model capable of long-horizon, whole-body locomotion and manipulation using generalist policies trained on whole-body human data.
The research demonstrates the model's ability to achieve complex everyday tasks such as operating a turntable and making the bed through coordinated movement and force interaction with objects.
This was accomplished by jointly designing the policy and controller, employing a delta action space to allow for seamless human intervention during execution.

The study highlights that long-horizon loco-manipulation presents significant challenges due to the coupled control, perception, and dynamic nature of the environment, emphasizing the importance of whole-body control and execution fidelity for reliable deployment.
This advancement indicates a significant step toward more capable and adaptable embodied artificial intelligence systems.
From technologyreview.com, "I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future. | MIT Technology Review".
This segment reports on a user experience with a humanoid robot cleaning service and its development process.
The key finding is that the robots are currently piloted remotely by humans using collected data for training autonomous capabilities.

The cleaning process involved the robots attempting tasks such as mopping and cleaning toilets, although navigation and task execution encountered difficulties, particularly when performing complex maneuvers like climbing stairs due to remote operation delays.
Despite these imperfections, the robots successfully completed the cleaning tasks, and the developing company intends to expand deployment to other job functions.
This progression indicates a move toward automating physical labor in the cleaning sector through advanced robotics.
From The Robot Report, "How Point One turned GPS accuracy into a robotics platform".
This story details how GPS accuracy has been transformed into a comprehensive robotics platform through the work of Point One Navigation.
The development centers on the integration of advanced sensor fusion and navigation techniques for robotic applications.
Point One Navigation is involved in this field and will host the FUSE 2026 physical AI event in San Francisco.
Aaron Nathan, the CEO of Point One Navigation, brings extensive experience in sensor fusion, computer vision, navigation, and embedded systems for robotics.
Nathan has led multidisciplinary teams across finance, defense, and enterprise sectors and has founded two venture-backed startups.
The discussion highlights the successful integration of GPS data into sophisticated robotic systems through rigorous data processing.
This advancement signifies a crucial step in creating highly accurate and navigable autonomous systems.
The integration of precise positioning data into robotics will accelerate the development of sophisticated AI-driven physical systems.
From The Robot Report, Industry experts discuss China blocking SoftBank's acquisition of ABB Robotics.
This story concerns the blockage of the acquisition due to concerns over the transfer of training data for artificial intelligence models overseas.
China initiated this action based on regulatory worries regarding the transfer of robotics data, which is now considered strategically important for physical AI development.
This regulatory action highlights broader concerns surrounding robotics data, intellectual property, and local manufacturing capabilities within cross-border mergers.
Other nations are also enacting measures to safeguard sovereign physical AI, exemplified by bans on certain autonomous robots in the United States.
This situation reflects escalating geopolitical tensions concerning the convergence of automation, data, and artificial intelligence.
The industry should monitor developments regarding cross-border data governance and autonomous technology regulations.
And that's all for today's circuit board update!
Wondering about the future of robotics, like that "Robot-as-a-Snap" mystery?
Keep those algorithms humming!
Until tomorrow, keep building brilliantly.
